claim: The olfactory placode has been classically presumed to form all olfactory sensory neurons.
source: Classically, it has been presumed that the olfactory placode forms all olfactory sensory neurons.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific consensus in the abstract.

claim: The cranial neural crest is the primary source of microvillous sensory neurons within the olfactory epithelium of zebrafish embryos.
source: In contrast, we show that the cranial neural crest is the primary source of microvillous sensory neurons within the olfactory epithelium of zebrafish embryos.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental approaches described throughout the manuscript.

claim: Neural crest precursors migrate from the neural tube to the nasal cavity.
source: Using photoconversion-based fate mapping and live cell tracking coupled with laser ablation, we followed neural crest precursors as they migrated from the neural tube to the nasal cavity.
evidence: This is directly observed through live imaging and fate mapping experiments.

claim: A subset of neural crest cells that coexpress Sox10 protein and a neurogenin1 reporter ingress into the olfactory epithelium and differentiate into microvillous sensory neurons.
source: A subset that coexpressed Sox10 protein and a neurogenin1 reporter ingressed into the olfactory epithelium and differentiated into microvillous sensory neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated through live imaging of double transgenic lines.

claim: Sox10 plays a critical role in microvillous neurogenesis.
source: Timed loss-of-function analysis revealed a critical role for Sox10 in microvillous neurogenesis.
evidence: This is demonstrated through morpholino knockdown experiments.

claim: The olfactory epithelium has remarkable ability to regenerate neurons in adult organisms.
source: This knowledge is critical for understanding not only disorders such as anosmia—the loss of smell—but also for clarifying the remarkable ability of the olfactory epithelium to regenerate neurons in adult organisms (Graziadei and Graziadei, 1979; Bermingham-McDonogh and Reh, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The peripheral nervous system of the vertebrate head is derived from cranial ectodermal placodes and neural crest cells.
source: The peripheral nervous system of the vertebrate head is derived from two sources: cranial ectodermal placodes and neural crest cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Placodes form the sense organs (nose, ears, and lens) of the head and contribute to neuronal portions of cranial ganglia.
source: Whereas placodes form the sense organs (nose, ears, and lens) of the head and contribute to neuronal portions of cranial ganglia, the glia are solely neural crest derived (Northcutt and Gans, 1983; Baker and Bronner-Fraser, 2001; Barraud et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Glia in cranial ganglia are solely neural crest derived.
source: Whereas placodes form the sense organs (nose, ears, and lens) of the head and contribute to neuronal portions of cranial ganglia, the glia are solely neural crest derived (Northcutt and Gans, 1983; Baker and Bronner-Fraser, 2001; Barraud et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The olfactory placode first becomes apparent around 18 hr post-fertilization (hpf) in zebrafish embryos.
source: In the zebrafish embryo, the olfactory placode first becomes apparent around 18 hr post-fertilization (hpf) (Hansen and Zeiske, 1993; Miyasaka et al., 2007) and subsequently gives rise to sensory neurons and supporting cell populations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The olfactory placode gives rise to sensory neurons and supporting cell populations.
source: In the zebrafish embryo, the olfactory placode first becomes apparent around 18 hr post-fertilization (hpf) (Hansen and Zeiske, 1993; Miyasaka et al., 2007) and subsequently gives rise to sensory neurons and supporting cell populations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: There are two predominant types of olfactory sensory neurons within the olfactory epithelium: ciliated and microvillous neurons.
source: Within the olfactory epithelium, there are two predominant types of olfactory sensory neurons: ciliated and microvillous neurons.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Ciliated and microvillous neurons differ in roles, receptors, location, and patterns of innervation.
source: These differ in roles, receptors, location, and patterns of innervation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Basally located ciliated sensory neurons detect volatile odorants.
source: Whereas more basally located ciliated sensory neurons detect volatile odorants, more apically located microvillous sensory neurons can detect pheromones, nucleotides, and/or amino acids, depending on the species (Buck, 2000; Sato and Suzuki, 2001; Hansen and Zielinski, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Apically located microvillous sensory neurons can detect pheromones, nucleotides, and/or amino acids, depending on the species.
source: Whereas more basally located ciliated sensory neurons detect volatile odorants, more apically located microvillous sensory neurons can detect pheromones, nucleotides, and/or amino acids, depending on the species (Buck, 2000; Sato and Suzuki, 2001; Hansen and Zielinski, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Olfactory ensheathing glia are neural crest derived.
source: Recent literature demonstrates that olfactory ensheathing glia, nonneuronal supporting cells previously assumed to derive from the olfactory epithelium, are actually neural crest derived (Barraud et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: All other peripheral glia are neural crest derived.
source: These findings are consistent with the neural crest origin of all other peripheral glia (Woodhoo and Sommer, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Some studies have suggested that neural crest cells give rise to GnRH cells of the terminal nerve.
source: As one example, some studies (Whitlock et al., 2003; Forni et al., 2011) have suggested that neural crest cells give rise to GnRH cells of the terminal nerve, which is close to though not part of the olfactory nerve and epithelium.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Many studies support a placodal origin for GnRH cells.
source: However, many other studies refute this notion and support a placodal origin for GnRH cells (Schwanzel-Fukuda and Pfaff, 1989; Wray et al., 1989; Dubois et al., 2002; Palevitch et al., 2007; Metz and Wray, 2010; Sabado et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Harden et al. (2012) interpreted their results to indicate a lack of contribution of neural crest cells to the olfactory epithelium.
source: Within the olfactory epithelium itself, Harden et al. (2012) recently examined the interactions of Sox10:eGFP-positive cells with six4b:mCherry-expressing placodal precursors in zebrafish. The authors interpreted their negative results to indicate a lack of contribution of neural crest cells to the olfactory epithelium.
evidence: This is a citation to previous literature with interpretation of their findings.

claim: Cranial neural crest cells move anteriorly from the dorsal neural tube toward the future location of the olfactory pit.
source: Visualization and analysis with Imaris software (Bitplane, Zurich, Switzerland) demonstrated that cranial neural crest cells moved anteriorly from the dorsal neural tube toward the future location of the olfactory pit.
evidence: This is demonstrated through live imaging analysis.

claim: Some neural crest cells migrate and coalesce as a cup-like structure around the olfactory vesicle to form the mesenchymal nasal cavity.
source: Some neural crest cells migrated and coalesced as a cup-like structure around the olfactory vesicle (Figure 1A,B) to form the mesenchymal nasal cavity, consistent with descriptions in mouse, chick, and medaka (Langille and Hall, 1988; Osumi-Yamashita et al., 1994; Le Douarin and Kalcheim, 1999).
evidence: This is demonstrated through live imaging and is consistent with previous literature in other species.

claim: Beginning at approximately 24 hpf and continuing until at least day 2, a subset of Sox10:eGFP-positive cells in the nasal cavity delaminate and intercalate into the olfactory epithelium.
source: Subsequently, beginning at ∼24 hpf and continuing until at least day 2, a subset of the Sox10:eGFP-positive cells in the nasal cavity delaminated and intercalated into the olfactory epithelium where placode-derived ciliated neurons and support cells were already present.
evidence: This is observed through live imaging experiments.

claim: Ingressing Sox10:eGFP-positive cells increase their eGFP levels and change their morphology from mesenchymal to the 'teardrop' shape characteristic of neurons.
source: Concomitantly, these cells increased their eGFP levels and changed their morphology from mesenchymal to the 'teardrop' shape characteristic of neurons (Figure 1C–J and Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is observed through live imaging experiments shown in figures and videos.

claim: All Sox10:eGFP-positive cells within the olfactory epithelium are microvillous neurons.
source: The results show that all of the Sox10:eGFP-positive cells within the olfactory epithelium are microvillous neurons, as revealed by their TRPC2:Venus expression and apical position (Figure 1K and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through colocalization experiments with TRPC2:Venus marker.

claim: None of the Sox10:eGFP-positive cells are OMP:RFP-positive ciliated neurons.
source: In contrast, none are OMP:RFP-positive ciliated neurons (data not shown).
evidence: This is demonstrated through marker analysis.

claim: A small number of microvillous neurons are Sox10:eGFP-negative.
source: A small number of microvillous neurons are Sox10:eGFP-negative (Figure 1K and Figure 1—figure Supplement 1, arrowheads), raising the possibility that a minor subset of these cells has a separate origin.
evidence: This is observed in imaging data and leads to speculation about their origin.

claim: A minor subset of microvillous neurons may have a separate origin from the neural crest.
source: A small number of microvillous neurons are Sox10:eGFP-negative (Figure 1K and Figure 1—figure Supplement 1, arrowheads), raising the possibility that a minor subset of these cells has a separate origin.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of Sox10:eGFP-negative microvillous neurons.

claim: Sox10:eGFP-positive neurons colocalize with HuC/D, a marker for newly born post-mitotic neurons.
source: To further confirm that the ingressed cells are neurons, we performed immunostaining with an antibody against HuC/D, a marker for newly born post-mitotic neurons (Kim et al., 1996), which colocalized in the apically located Sox10:eGFP-positive neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunostaining experiments.

claim: All neurogenic placodes in zebrafish, including the olfactory placode, express the proneural bHLH transcription factor Ngn1.
source: All neurogenic placodes in zebrafish, including the olfactory placode, express the proneural bHLH transcription factor Ngn1, which is known to be required for sensory neuron differentiation in mice (Andermann et al., 2002; Bertrand et al., 2002; Cau et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Ngn1 is required for sensory neuron differentiation in mice.
source: All neurogenic placodes in zebrafish, including the olfactory placode, express the proneural bHLH transcription factor Ngn1, which is known to be required for sensory neuron differentiation in mice (Andermann et al., 2002; Bertrand et al., 2002; Cau et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Ngn1 is expressed in neural crest cells that become sensory neurons in the dorsal root ganglia in zebrafish.
source: In addition, Ngn1 is expressed in neural crest cells that become sensory neurons in the dorsal root ganglia in zebrafish (McGraw et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Ngn1:nRFP is expressed in a subset of Sox10:eGFP-positive cells in the nasal cavity.
source: Using a Ngn1:nRFP transgenic line (Blader et al., 2003) that has been well-characterized as representative of endogenous Ngn1 expression (Blader et al., 2003, 2004; Madelaine et al., 2011), we noted Ngn1:nRFP expression in a subset of Sox10:eGFP-positive cells in the nasal cavity (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is observed through imaging of double transgenic lines.

claim: Only cells that upregulate Sox10:eGFP and coexpress Ngn1:nRFP ingress into the olfactory epithelium to differentiate into microvillous neurons.
source: Interestingly, only cells that upregulate Sox10:eGFP and coexpress Ngn1:nRFP ingress into the olfactory epithelium to differentiate into microvillous neurons (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is observed through live imaging of double transgenic lines.

claim: Photoconversion was performed between 14 hpf (10-somite stage) and 16 hpf (14-somite stage), always unilaterally.
source: In both cases, all photoconversion was performed between 14 hpf (10-somite stage) and 16 hpf (14-somite stage), always unilaterally.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: Prior to day 1 of development, no photoconverted cells were observed in the olfactory epithelium.
source: Prior to day 1 of development, no photoconverted cells were observed in the olfactory epithelium (data not shown), consistent with our previous findings from the Sox10 reporter line on the timing of microvillous ingression (see Figure 1).
evidence: This is an observation from photoconversion experiments.

claim: At 29 hpf, a few photoconverted cells were present in the nasal cavity.
source: At 29 hpf, a few photoconverted cells were present in the nasal cavity (Figure 2D–E').
evidence: This is observed in photoconversion experiments.

claim: At 55 hpf, photoconverted neural crest cells had differentiated into apically localized microvillous neurons.
source: At 55 hpf, by which time ingression/differentiation was nearly complete, photoconverted neural crest cells had differentiated into apically localized microvillous neurons.
evidence: This is observed in photoconversion experiments.

claim: No photoconverted cells differentiate into basally located ciliated neurons.
source: In contrast, no photoconverted cells differentiate into the basally located ciliated neurons, consistent with their placodal origin and confirming the specificity of our labeling.
evidence: This is observed in photoconversion experiments and confirms specificity.

claim: Many labeled neural crest cells cross the midline and migrate to the contralateral side where they differentiate into microvillous neurons.
source: Interestingly, many labeled neural crest cells cross the midline and migrate to the contralateral side (shown in Figure 2) where they differentiate into microvillous neurons.
evidence: This is observed in photoconversion experiments.

claim: The olfactory epithelium is unable to compensate for the loss of neural crest-derived microvillous neurons.
source: Taken together, these results reveal an essential role for a specific subset of neural crest–derived cells in the nasal cavity that upregulate Ngn1 shortly before ingressing into the olfactory epithelium. Interestingly, the placode-derived olfactory epithelium is unable to compensate for the loss of the neural crest–derived population of microvillous neurons.
evidence: This is concluded from laser ablation experiments.

claim: Two-photon laser ablation was performed at 25 hpf unilaterally on small (2–7 cells) or large (≥20 cells) groups of neural crest-derived nasal cavity cells.
source: Two-photon laser ablation was performed at 25 hpf unilaterally on small (2–7 cells, not shown) or large (≥20 cells) (Figure 3A,B) groups of neural crest-derived nasal cavity cells that were Sox10:eGFP positive and either Ngn1:nRFP negative or positive.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: By 35 hpf, both small and large ablations of Ngn1:nRFP-positive cells in the right-side nasal cavity had highly deleterious effects on the subsequent number of microvillous neurons.
source: By 35 hpf, both the small (Figure 3C) and large (Figure 3D) ablations of Ngn1:nRFP-positive cells in the right-side nasal cavity had highly deleterious effects on the subsequent number of microvillous neurons.
evidence: This is observed in laser ablation experiments.

claim: Large ablations often produced a striking phenotype with the near-complete absence of microvillous neurogenesis post-ablation.
source: Large ablations often produced a striking phenotype with the near-complete absence of microvillous neurogenesis post-ablation (Figure 3D), whereas placode-derived ciliated neurons (Sox10:eGFP negative and Ngn1:nRFP positive in olfactory epithelium) continued to form.
evidence: This is observed in laser ablation experiments.

claim: Placode-derived ciliated neurons continued to form after ablation of neural crest cells.
source: Large ablations often produced a striking phenotype with the near-complete absence of microvillous neurogenesis post-ablation (Figure 3D), whereas placode-derived ciliated neurons (Sox10:eGFP negative and Ngn1:nRFP positive in olfactory epithelium) continued to form.
evidence: This is observed in laser ablation experiments.

claim: Ablations of Ngn1:nRFP-negative nasal cavity cells had a minor phenotype.
source: Ablations of Ngn1:nRFP-negative nasal cavity cells had a minor phenotype (data not shown), which may be due to the fact that some ablated cells were destined to turn on Ngn1 but were not yet expressing Ngn1:nRFP at detectable levels.
evidence: This is observed in laser ablation experiments with speculation about the reason.

claim: Sox10 protein levels markedly increase in differentiating neural crest-derived microvillous neurons as they move from the nasal cavity into the olfactory epithelium.
source: These experiments reveal a marked increase in Sox10 protein levels in differentiating neural crest–derived microvillous neurons as they move from the nasal cavity (arrowhead) into the olfactory epithelium and transition from mesenchymal to the teardrop morphology characteristic of neurons at both 26 and 34 hpf (Figure 4A–B').
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunostaining experiments.

claim: Directly adjacent ciliated neurons do not upregulate Sox10.
source: Directly adjacent ciliated neurons (unstained) do not upregulate Sox10.
evidence: This is observed in immunostaining experiments.

claim: Loss of Sox10 leads to marked depletion of microvillous neurons in the olfactory epithelium.
source: The results show that loss of Sox10 leads to marked depletion of microvillous neurons in the olfactory epithelium (Figure 5B,C',E',F',H) in comparison to control morpholino-treated embryos (Figure 5A',D',G).
evidence: This is demonstrated through morpholino knockdown experiments.

claim: Neighboring ciliated neurons develop with only mild disruption after Sox10 knockdown.
source: Neighboring ciliated neurons, in contrast, develop with only mild disruption (Figure 5B,C,E,F), suggesting that downregulation of Sox10 protein specifically affects formation of microvillous neurons.
evidence: This is observed in morpholino knockdown experiments.

claim: Downregulation of Sox10 protein specifically affects formation of microvillous neurons.
source: Neighboring ciliated neurons, in contrast, develop with only mild disruption (Figure 5B,C,E,F), suggesting that downregulation of Sox10 protein specifically affects formation of microvillous neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects on microvillous versus ciliated neurons.

claim: The Sox10 morpholino phenotype was apparent as early as 29 hpf and remained consistent at 33 hpf, 55 hpf, and beyond.
source: This phenotype was apparent as early as 29 hpf (Figure 5A–C') and remained consistent at 33 hpf, 55 hpf, and beyond (Figure 5D–H and Figure 5–figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observed in morpholino knockdown experiments over time.

claim: By 55 hpf, ciliated neurons were present in robust numbers comparable to those in control embryos after Sox10 knockdown.
source: By 55 hpf, ciliated neurons were present in robust numbers comparable to those in the control embryos, while microvillous neurons remained scarce and those that did form appeared disorganized.
evidence: This is observed in morpholino knockdown experiments.

claim: After Sox10 knockdown, microvillous neurons remained scarce and those that did form appeared disorganized.
source: By 55 hpf, ciliated neurons were present in robust numbers comparable to those in the control embryos, while microvillous neurons remained scarce and those that did form appeared disorganized.
evidence: This is observed in morpholino knockdown experiments.

claim: The few remaining microvillous neurons after Sox10 knockdown were often TRPC2:Venus positive but Sox10:eGFP negative.
source: Furthermore, the few remaining microvillous neurons were often TRPC2:Venus positive but Sox10:eGFP negative (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that they were likely the small proportion of microvillous neurons not derived from the neural crest.
evidence: This is observed in morpholino knockdown experiments and leads to inference about their origin.

claim: The remaining microvillous neurons after Sox10 knockdown were likely the small proportion of microvillous neurons not derived from the neural crest.
source: Furthermore, the few remaining microvillous neurons were often TRPC2:Venus positive but Sox10:eGFP negative (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that they were likely the small proportion of microvillous neurons not derived from the neural crest.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that remaining microvillous neurons lack Sox10:eGFP.

claim: Sox10 loss leads to a known 'colorless' phenotype due to its necessity for melanocyte differentiation.
source: Since Sox10 is necessary for differentiation of many neural crest lineages, including the melanocyte lineage, its loss leads to a known 'colorless' phenotype (Dutton et al., 2001a, 2001b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Decrease in pigmentation can be used as a surrogate marker for the degree of Sox10 knockdown.
source: We were able to use this decrease in pigmentation as a surrogate marker for the degree of Sox10 knockdown.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known relationship between Sox10 and pigmentation.

claim: Microvillous neuron reduction is a consistent and common feature across all categories after knockdown of Sox10.
source: Surprisingly, microvillous neuron reduction is a consistent and common feature across all categories after knockdown of Sox10.
evidence: This is observed across different phenotypic categories in morpholino experiments.

claim: Microvillous neuron formation is exquisitely sensitive to reductions in Sox10 protein levels.
source: These data suggest that microvillous neuron formation is exquisitely sensitive to reductions in Sox10 protein levels, whereas other Sox10-dependent processes such as pigmentation may be more resilient.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that microvillous neurons are affected even when pigmentation is less affected.

claim: Other Sox10-dependent processes such as pigmentation may be more resilient to Sox10 reduction than microvillous neuron formation.
source: These data suggest that microvillous neuron formation is exquisitely sensitive to reductions in Sox10 protein levels, whereas other Sox10-dependent processes such as pigmentation may be more resilient.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential sensitivity of different Sox10-dependent processes.

claim: Sox10 plays a variety of roles in neural crest development that differ in time and cell type.
source: The transcription factor Sox10 plays a variety of roles in neural crest development that differ in time and cell type.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Knockdown of Sox10 expression at 24 hpf specifically impeded microvillous neuron formation and organization.
source: While control embryos developed normal numbers and organization of olfactory sensory neurons at 38 hpf (Figure 6A,A') and 54 hpf (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), knockdown of Sox10 expression at 24 hpf specifically impeded microvillous neuron formation and organization (Figure 6B,B' and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through photo-morpholino experiments.

claim: Knockdown at 17.5 hpf had an even more pronounced effect than knockdown at 24 hpf.
source: Knockdown at the earlier 17.5 hpf time point had an even more pronounced effect (data not shown), since it allowed more time for degradation of existing Sox10 protein before the start of ingression.
evidence: This is observed in photo-morpholino experiments with reasoning provided.

claim: The 24 hpf time point of photocleavage occurs well after neural crest cells have populated the nasal cavity.
source: Importantly, the later 24 hpf time point of photocleavage occurs well after neural crest cells have populated the nasal cavity, and results from that experiment decouple microvillous neurogenesis from earlier, critical roles of Sox10 in neural crest development and migration.
evidence: This is inferred from the timing of neural crest migration and the experimental design.

claim: Sox10 is required for ingression/differentiation from the nasal cavity into the olfactory epithelium to generate microvillous neurons.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that Sox10 is required for ingression/differentiation from the nasal cavity into the olfactory epithelium to generate microvillous neurons.
evidence: This is concluded from photo-morpholino experiments.

claim: Sox10 is required for formation of sensory, sympathetic, and enteric neurons as well as glia and Schwann cells.
source: Sox10 is not only required for formation of sensory, sympathetic, and enteric neurons but also for glia and Schwann cells (Britsch et al., 2001; Sonnenberg-Riethmacher et al., 2001; Carney et al., 2006; Kelsh, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Sox10's expression in and specific effect on microvillous neurons within the first several hours of olfactogenesis demonstrate a direct effect on neurogenesis.
source: Data shown here, namely Sox10's expression in and specific effect on microvillous neurons within the first several hours of olfactogenesis, demonstrate a direct effect on neurogenesis at least in the context of zebrafish olfactory development.
evidence: This is inferred from the timing and specificity of Sox10's effects observed in the experiments.

claim: It was long assumed that olfactory sensory neurons derive solely from the olfactory placode.
source: It was long assumed that olfactory sensory neurons derive solely from the olfactory placode (Hansen and Zeiske, 1993; Whitlock and Westerfield, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Two lineage analysis studies in mice suggested that a small subpopulation of unspecified olfactory sensory neurons may have a neural crest origin.
source: Although two lineage analysis studies in mice suggested that a small subpopulation of unspecified olfactory sensory neurons may have a neural crest origin (Forni et al., 2011; Katoh et al., 2011), they relied upon Wnt1-Cre and P0-Cre, both of which suffer from lack of neural crest specificity.
evidence: This is a citation to previous literature with critique of their methods.

claim: Wnt1-Cre and P0-Cre both suffer from lack of neural crest specificity.
source: Although two lineage analysis studies in mice suggested that a small subpopulation of unspecified olfactory sensory neurons may have a neural crest origin (Forni et al., 2011; Katoh et al., 2011), they relied upon Wnt1-Cre and P0-Cre, both of which suffer from lack of neural crest specificity.
evidence: This is stated as a critique of previous methods.

claim: Conflicting work using Wnt1-Cre lineage tracing found no contribution to neurons but rather a neural crest contribution only to olfactory ensheathing glia.
source: Furthermore, conflicting work by another group also using Wnt1-Cre lineage tracing found no contribution to neurons but rather a neural crest contribution only to olfactory ensheathing glia (Barraud et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a citation to previous literature.

claim: The Wnt1 marker is not entirely neural crest specific, as it is also expressed in the dorsal neural tube, otic placode, and several other regions.
source: Interpretation of these experiments is made difficult by the fact that the Wnt1 marker is not entirely neural crest specific, as it is also expressed in the dorsal neural tube, otic placode, and several other regions (Riccomagno et al., 2005; Liu et al., 2006; Freyer et al., 2011; Valenta et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Harden et al. (2012) suggest the idea of a possible neural crest contribution to olfactory ensheathing glia but not to sensory neurons, although they provide no direct evidence to substantiate this possibility.
source: In zebrafish, Harden et al. (2012) suggest the idea of a possible neural crest contribution to olfactory ensheathing glia but not to sensory neurons, although they provide no direct evidence to substantiate this possibility.
evidence: This is a citation to previous literature with critique.

claim: By using photoconversion of Sox10-expressing neural crest cells, individual neural crest cells can be unequivocally followed from their site of origin in the dorsal neural tube to their ingression into the olfactory epithelium and differentiation into microvillous sensory neurons.
source: Here, by using photoconversion of Sox10-expressing neural crest cells, we were able to unequivocally follow individual neural crest cells from their site of origin in the dorsal neural tube to their ingression into the olfactory epithelium and differentiation into microvillous sensory neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated through photoconversion experiments.

claim: Olfactory sensory neurons are notable for their regenerative capacity.
source: Olfactory sensory neurons are notable for their regenerative capacity.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Analysis of olfactory neuron lineage, paths of differentiation, and molecular determinants may provide important insights into general mechanisms of self-renewal.
source: Hence, analysis of their lineage, paths of differentiation, and molecular determinants may provide important insights into general mechanisms of self-renewal.
evidence: This is speculation about the broader implications of the research.

claim: Processes of renewal may be lineage-dependent.
source: Since processes of renewal may be lineage-dependent, understanding the embryonic origins of different classes of olfactory neurons has distinct value.
evidence: This is speculation about the importance of lineage in regeneration.

claim: Replenishment of placode-derived ciliated sensory neurons throughout the lifespan likely occurs within the mature olfactory vesicle.
source: In the case of placode-derived ciliated sensory neurons, their replenishment throughout the lifespan likely occurs within the mature olfactory vesicle.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of ciliated neuron renewal.

claim: There may be a subpopulation of microvillous sensory neurons derived from the olfactory vesicle.
source: Similarly, there may be a subpopulation of microvillous sensory neurons derived from the olfactory vesicle.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of Sox10:eGFP-negative microvillous neurons.

claim: Replacement of microvillous neurons during adulthood may take place via a latent neural crest stem cell population derived from the nasal cavity.
source: Alternatively, given our evidence of large-scale neural crest contribution to microvillous sensory neurons, it is intriguing to consider that their replacement during adulthood may take place via a latent neural crest stem cell population derived from the nasal cavity.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of microvillous neuron renewal in adults.

claim: During vertebrate evolution, a myriad of changes have occurred in olfaction, including the emergence of the vomeronasal organ.
source: During vertebrate evolution, a myriad of changes have occurred in olfaction, including the emergence of the vomeronasal organ, which fish and birds appear to lack.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Fish and birds appear to lack the vomeronasal organ.
source: During vertebrate evolution, a myriad of changes have occurred in olfaction, including the emergence of the vomeronasal organ, which fish and birds appear to lack.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: It will be interesting to examine possible neural crest contributions to olfaction from a comparative perspective as new lineage tracing tools become available in other model systems.
source: Given the diverse nature of olfaction across species, it will be interesting to examine possible neural crest contributions from a comparative perspective as new lineage tracing tools become available in other model systems.
evidence: This is speculation about future research directions.
